Intersection bodies represent a remarkable class of geometric objects associated with sections of star bodies and invoking   Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and the relevant Fourier analysis. The main focus of this article is interrelation between generalized cosine transforms of different kinds in the context of their application to investigation of a certain family of intersection bodies, which we call $\lam$-intersection bodies. The latter include $k$-intersection bodies (in the sense of A. Koldobsky) and unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of $L_p$-spaces. In particular, we show that restrictions onto lower dimensional subspaces of the spherical Radon transforms and the generalized cosine transforms preserve their integral-geometric structure. We apply this result to the study of sections of $\lam$-intersection bodies. New characterizations of this class of bodies are obtained and examples are given. We also review some known facts and give them new proofs.

The main focus of this article is the interrelation between different kinds of generalized cosine transforms in the context of their application to the investigation of a certain family of intersection bodies, which we call $\lam$-intersection bodies. This article primarily examines how different types of generalized cosine transforms are related, especially in their use for studying a particular class of intersection bodies that we call \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. This class contains \(k\)-intersection bodies, in A. Koldobsky’s sense, as well as unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\) spaces.  

In particular, we prove that when spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms are restricted to lower-dimensional subspaces, their integral-geometric structure is maintained. Intersection bodies are important geometric objects in convex and integral geometry. They are closely related to the study of sections of star bodies and arise naturally through tools such as spherical Radon transforms, generalized cosine transforms, and Fourier analysis. These connections make intersection bodies useful in problems concerning volume, sections, and embeddings of normed spaces.

The article investigates relationships between several types of generalized cosine transforms and explores how these relationships can be applied to a broad class of geometric objects known as \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. This class provides a flexible framework that unifies and extends several earlier notions. In particular, \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies include Koldobsky’s \(k\)-intersection bodies, which play a central role in the study of lower-dimensional sections, as well as unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\)-spaces.

A central theme of the article is the behavior of integral transforms under restriction to lower-dimensional subspaces. The authors prove that when spherical Radon transforms and generalized cosine transforms are restricted in this way, they retain their essential integral-geometric structure. In other words, the restricted transforms can still be understood as transforms of the same general type, but now acting within the smaller subspace. This observation provides a powerful mechanism for transferring results from the ambient space to its subspaces.

Using these structural results, the article studies sections of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The authors obtain new characterizations of such sections and give examples illustrating the scope of the theory. Their approach also yields new proofs of several known results, showing that many facts about intersection bodies and related classes can be understood more transparently through the interaction between generalized cosine transforms, Radon transforms, and subspace restrictions.

Overall, the work deepens the connection between convex geometry, harmonic analysis, and integral geometry. It demonstrates that \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies form a natural and robust family of geometric objects whose properties are well suited to analysis by generalized transform methods.

The article investigates the interplay between generalized cosine transforms, spherical Radon transforms, and Fourier-analytic methods in the study of convex and star bodies, with particular emphasis on the class of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. This class provides a unified framework for several important objects in convex geometry, including Koldobsky’s \(k\)-intersection bodies and unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\) spaces. By placing these bodies in a common analytic and integral-geometric setting, the article clarifies how different notions of intersection bodies are connected and how they can be characterized through transform methods.

A central theme of the work is the behavior of integral transforms when restricted to lower-dimensional subspaces. The article shows that generalized cosine transforms and spherical Radon transforms retain their essential structural properties under such restrictions. More precisely, the restriction of these transforms to sections or subspaces can be described in terms of corresponding transforms on lower-dimensional spheres. This compatibility makes it possible to pass between global information on the ambient sphere and local information on subspheres, preserving the integral-geometric meaning of the transforms involved.

These restriction results are then applied to the theory of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The article proves new characterizations of such bodies in terms of generalized cosine transforms, spherical Radon transforms, and Fourier transforms of homogeneous distributions. These characterizations extend and unify earlier descriptions of \(k\)-intersection bodies and related classes. In particular, they show that many structural properties of intersection bodies are stable under passage to lower-dimensional subspaces, which leads to new examples and broader inclusion results.

The Fourier-analytic approach plays an important role throughout the article. By translating geometric questions about radial functions, sections, and volumes into statements about distributions and their Fourier transforms, the paper obtains streamlined proofs of several known theorems. At the same time, it derives new results concerning the existence and construction of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. This approach highlights the deep connection between convex geometry, harmonic analysis on the sphere, and the theory of integral transforms.

Overall, the article demonstrates that generalized cosine transforms and spherical Radon transforms provide powerful and flexible tools for understanding intersection-type bodies. The main results show that these transforms behave naturally under restriction to subspaces and that this behavior leads to new characterizations, examples, and proofs in the theory of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. In doing so, the work both extends existing results and offers a more unified analytic framework for studying important classes of bodies arising in convex geometry and the geometry of Banach spaces.

**Intersection, Radon, and Fourier**

The ideas of *intersection*, the *Radon transform*, and the *Fourier transform* are deeply connected in geometry, analysis, and imaging. Together, they provide powerful ways to describe objects, recover hidden structures, and understand how information is distributed across space and frequency.

An **intersection** usually refers to the set of points shared by geometric objects. In integral geometry, intersections are often studied through lines, planes, or higher-dimensional slices passing through a body or function. Instead of examining an object directly, one can study how it intersects with many lines or hyperplanes. These intersections reveal important information about the shape, density, or internal structure of the object.

The **Radon transform** formalizes this idea. Given a function defined on a space, the Radon transform records its integrals over hyperplanes. In two dimensions, for example, it integrates a function over straight lines. This is the mathematical foundation of computed tomography, such as CT scans: X-rays measure the total absorption of tissue along many lines through the body, and these line integrals are used to reconstruct an image of the interior.

The **Fourier transform** is another fundamental tool. It decomposes a function into its frequency components, showing how much of each oscillatory pattern is present. The Fourier transform is central in signal processing, physics, and partial differential equations because it converts many complicated spatial operations into simpler algebraic ones in frequency space.

The connection between the Radon and Fourier transforms is expressed by the **Fourier slice theorem**. This theorem states that the one-dimensional Fourier transform of a Radon projection of a function equals a slice of the multidimensional Fourier transform of that function. In other words, projections obtained by the Radon transform correspond to intersections, or slices, of the Fourier transform in frequency space.

This relationship is essential in image reconstruction. By collecting many Radon projections from different angles, one obtains many Fourier slices. Combining these slices makes it possible to reconstruct the original function or image. Thus, intersection geometry, Radon transforms, and Fourier analysis come together in a single framework with important applications in medicine, engineering, physics, and data science.

Building on harmonic-analytic methods, we analyze a family of cosine-type operators depending on a complex parameter and relate their meromorphic continuation, spectral decomposition on spherical harmonics, and inversion properties to corresponding Radon transforms on Grassmannians. These operator identities are then applied to the definition and characterization of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies, a parameterized class extending classical intersection bodies. In particular, we establish equivalences between positivity conditions for generalized cosine transforms, Radon-transform representations of radial functions, and membership in classes of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. The results provide a unified framework connecting spherical integral geometry, distributional Fourier analysis, and geometric properties of star bodies, and yield new analytic criteria for recognizing intersection-type structures in convex geometry.

This abstract examines the role of generalized cosine transforms in the analytic and geometric theory of intersection bodies and their extensions. Generalized cosine transforms, acting on functions or measures on spheres and Grassmannians, provide a unifying integral-geometric framework for studying star bodies, projection-type operators, and dualities in convex geometry. Their spectral properties, intertwining relations with Radon transforms, and analytic continuation in the transform parameter are central to understanding when geometric data determine a body and when positivity of associated distributions characterizes membership in special body classes.

Particular attention is given to the connection between these transforms and \(k\)-intersection bodies, which generalize Lutwak’s classical intersection bodies by replacing hyperplane sections with sections of higher codimension. In this setting, spherical and Grassmannian cosine transforms encode the passage from radial functions of star bodies to volumes of sections, while their range and positivity properties yield criteria for a body to be a \(k\)-intersection body. These criteria are closely related to the behavior of invariant distributions under fractional powers of the Laplacian and to generalized Radon transforms on Grassmann manifolds.

The abstract also highlights the relationship between intersection-body theory and finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\), especially for negative values of \(p\). Through Fourier-analytic characterizations, a normed space embeds in \(L_p\) for certain negative \(p\) precisely when powers of its norm define positive definite distributions. This condition parallels the positivity conditions arising from generalized cosine transforms and links \(k\)-intersection bodies to embeddings in \(L_{-k}\). Thus, generalized cosine transforms serve as a bridge between convex geometric tomography, harmonic analysis on homogeneous spaces, and the local theory of Banach spaces.

Overall, the study of these transforms clarifies the structural hierarchy among intersection bodies, \(k\)-intersection bodies, and related classes of star bodies, while also providing analytic tools for addressing section problems such as the Busemann–Petty problem and its higher-codimensional variants.

We study \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) through the behavior of spherical Radon and cosine transforms under restriction to lower-dimensional subspaces. Extending the classical framework of intersection bodies, we analyze how generalized radial data associated with a star body \(K\) is encoded by transform identities on \(S^{n-1}\), and how these identities descend to subspheres \(S^{m-1}=S^{n-1}\cap E\), where \(E\in G_{n,m}\). In particular, we establish restriction formulas relating the ambient Radon and cosine transforms to their intrinsic counterparts on \(E\), with explicit dependence on the parameter \(\lambda\) and the codimension.

These formulas yield structural results for sections of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies. We show that, under natural admissibility conditions on \(\lambda\), central sections of a \(\lambda\)-intersection body are again generalized intersection bodies of corresponding order in the lower-dimensional subspace. Conversely, we identify obstructions to such inheritance when the relevant transform ranges fail to be stable under restriction. The results provide a unified analytic approach to section phenomena for intersection-type bodies, connecting Fourier-analytic characterizations, spherical integral geometry, and convex-geometric stability properties.

As applications, we derive consequences for volume comparison problems of Busemann–Petty type in lower dimensions, describe the behavior of associated section functions, and obtain criteria ensuring that geometric inequalities for \(K\) pass to its central sections. The paper clarifies the role of restricted Radon and cosine transforms in the local theory of \(\lambda\)-intersection bodies and offers a framework for studying higher-codimensional sections via harmonic analysis on the sphere.

Working in the setting of origin-symmetric star bodies in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), we relate geometric positivity conditions on radial functions to analytic positivity properties of associated distributions and integral transforms on the sphere. In particular, we formulate criteria identifying when a star body belongs to generalized classes of intersection bodies in terms of the range and positivity structure of higher-order Radon transforms and \(\lambda\)-cosine transforms. These criteria extend classical Fourier characterizations of intersection bodies and provide a unified framework encompassing \(k\)-intersection bodies, generalized intersection bodies, and related dual mixed-volume constructions.  

A central feature of the approach is the systematic use of analytic continuation and inversion formulas for cosine-type transforms, which allows one to pass between spherical data, section-volume functions, and homogeneous distributions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). We obtain necessary and sufficient conditions expressed through positive measures, positive definite distributions, and transform inequalities on \(S^{n-1}\). As applications, we derive new equivalences for membership in intersection-type classes, clarify the relationship between Radon-transform ranges and Fourier positivity, and indicate consequences for Busemann–Petty-type comparison problems. The results highlight the role of generalized cosine transforms as a bridge between convex-geometric structure and harmonic analysis on the sphere.

## A concise summary: Intersection bodies, cosine transforms, \(k\)-intersection bodies, and \(L_p\)-balls

Intersection body theory is a central part of asymptotic convex geometry, originating in Lutwak’s reformulation of the Busemann–Petty problem. For an origin-symmetric star body \(K\subset \mathbb{R}^n\), its intersection body \(IK\) is defined by the radial function  
\[
\rho_{IK}(\xi)=\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(K\cap \xi^\perp),\qquad \xi\in S^{n-1}.
\]
Thus the radius of \(IK\) in direction \(\xi\) records the hyperplane section volume of \(K\) orthogonal to \(\xi\). This construction connects convex geometry with harmonic analysis through the spherical Radon transform.

A broader framework is obtained using generalized cosine transforms. For suitable functions or measures on the Grassmannian \(G_{n,m}\), these transforms integrate powers of the cosine of principal angles between subspaces. They provide an analytic language for section-volume operators and allow one to describe intersection-type bodies via integral transforms rather than only geometric section data. In particular, the classical spherical Radon transform appears as a limiting or special case.

The notion of a \(k\)-intersection body generalizes Lutwak’s intersection bodies by replacing hyperplane sections with sections of codimension \(k\). A star body \(D\) is a \(k\)-intersection body if its radial function satisfies a representation of the form  
\[
\rho_D^k(\xi)=\operatorname{vol}_{n-k}(K\cap \xi^\perp),
\]
or, more generally, if \(\rho_D^k\) lies in the range or closure of an appropriate Grassmannian Radon-type transform. These bodies are important in the generalized Busemann–Petty problem, where one asks whether inequalities for all lower-dimensional sections imply inequalities for total volume.

The theory also interacts strongly with \(L_p\)-balls. Unit balls of finite-dimensional subspaces of \(L_p\), especially for \(0<p\leq 2\), often possess intersection-body-type structure. Fourier-analytic criteria show that many such bodies are \(k\)-intersection bodies because powers of their Minkowski functionals define positive definite distributions. This links section inequalities, embeddings into \(L_p\), and convex-geometric transform theory.

Recent results deepen the integral-geometric structure behind these objects. They identify new classes of star bodies whose section functions admit representations through generalized cosine transforms on Grassmannians. Such results clarify when a body is a \(k\)-intersection body, when it belongs to a larger transform-generated class, and how section-volume data determine or constrain radial functions. New section inequalities also emerge: under suitable positivity or transform-representation assumptions, comparison of all codimension-\(k\) sections yields comparison of volumes or mixed volumes.

Overall, the modern picture is that intersection bodies and their \(k\)-dimensional analogues are best understood through a combination of spherical analysis, generalized cosine transforms, and Grassmannian integral geometry. This framework unifies classical section problems, Fourier criteria for \(L_p\)-balls, and newer structural theorems describing how lower-dimensional sections encode global geometric information.
